questions.stem: A process loads a warehouse table with thousands of single-row INSERT statements and is slow. What is the better pattern?

options.text: Add more single-row inserts running in parallel across several connections
Load in batches with COPY INTO, INSERT ... SELECT or CREATE TABLE AS SELECT
Wrap each single-row insert in its own explicit BEGIN TRAN and COMMIT
Use a cursor

questions.explanation: The warehouse is built for set-based loads. Singleton inserts create many small files and transactions.

questions.stem: What does the warehouse do about statistics for the query optimizer?

options.text: You must rebuild every clustered and nonclustered index nightly so the optimizer has fresh statistics
It creates and updates statistics automatically, and you can also create them manually for specific columns
It needs a scheduled Spark job to compute statistics from the Delta log before the optimizer can use any of them
Nothing; the warehouse's optimizer doesn't use statistics, so plans rely only on table size

questions.explanation: Statistics help the optimizer estimate row counts. The warehouse maintains them automatically, and manual statistics can help specific queries.

questions.stem: Why should warehouse columns use the smallest data type that fits the values, such as varchar(50) instead of varchar(8000)?

options.text: Larger types such as varchar(8000) are not allowed in a Fabric warehouse
It makes no difference, since storage is compressed to the real value length
Smaller types make storage, memory use and query processing more efficient
Smaller types turn on V-Order for the column, which compresses it better

questions.explanation: Right-sized types reduce what has to be stored, read and held in memory, which speeds up queries.

questions.stem: Files in a storage account must be loaded into a warehouse table as fast as possible. What should you use?

options.text: COPY INTO
A loop of single-row INSERTs
SELECT INTO a temp table, row by row
A cursor over the file

questions.explanation: COPY INTO loads files into warehouse tables at high throughput.

questions.stem: A warehouse query is slow the first time it runs after a load, then fast. In queryinsights.exec_requests_history, which column tells you that a cold start affected the first run?

options.text: A nonzero `data_scanned_remote_storage_mb`
A nonzero `result_cache_hit` on the first run
A zero `row_count` for the first run
A `status` of Canceled on the first run

questions.explanation: A nonzero data_scanned_remote_storage_mb means data was read from remote storage, which indicates a cold start. result_cache_hit is about result set caching.

questions.stem: You load CSV files from Azure Data Lake Storage into several warehouse tables with COPY INTO. Which two practices maximize throughput? Each correct answer is a complete solution.

options.text: Convert the files to many single-row INSERT statements
Split the data into thousands of 1 MB files
Run multiple COPY INTO statements in parallel to load different tables
Load all tables with one COPY INTO statement after another in a single session
Make each file ideally between 100 MB and 1 GB

questions.explanation: The guidance asks for files of 100 MB to 1 GB and parallel COPY INTO statements into different tables. Tiny files and single-row inserts hurt performance.

questions.stem: A team wants to disable V-Order on a write-heavy staging warehouse to reduce ingestion overhead. What must they know first?

options.text: V-Order can only be disabled per table, not per warehouse
Disabling V-Order also turns off automatic statistics
Once V-Order is disabled on a warehouse, it can't be re-enabled
Disabling V-Order deletes the warehouse's query insights history

questions.explanation: V-Order adds a small ingestion overhead, but disabling it on a warehouse is permanent. The other statements aren't in the guidance.

questions.stem: Reports use a lakehouse table through its SQL analytics endpoint. After many small writes the queries slow down. What should you do?

options.text: Run UPDATE STATISTICS on the SQL analytics endpoint every hour to fix the plans for all the small files
Disable result set caching on the SQL analytics endpoint so each query reads the newest files
Wait, because automatic data compaction runs on lakehouse tables too, as it does in the warehouse
Run OPTIMIZE on the lakehouse table, because warehouse data compaction doesn't apply to the lakehouse

questions.explanation: Data compaction runs automatically for Fabric Data Warehouse but doesn't apply to the lakehouse; for lakehouse tables you run OPTIMIZE after big changes.

questions.stem: A warehouse table was created with `CLUSTER BY (CustomerId)`, but most queries now filter on SaleDate. How do you change the clustering column?

options.text: Run `UPDATE STATISTICS` on SaleDate so the clustering follows it
Create a new table with CTAS and `WITH (CLUSTER BY (SaleDate))`
Run `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (SaleDate)` on the existing table
Use `SELECT INTO` a new table with a `CLUSTER BY (SaleDate)` clause

questions.explanation: Clustering columns can't be changed after creation; you use CTAS to create a new table with the desired clustering. SELECT INTO with data clustering isn't supported.

questions.stem: You choose a data clustering column for a large warehouse fact table. Which column is the best candidate?

options.text: An IDENTITY column used as the fact table's surrogate key
A low cardinality column such as a two-value IsActive flag
A mid-to-high cardinality column used often in WHERE predicates
A column used only in equality join conditions to dimension tables

questions.explanation: Mid-to-high cardinality columns that appear often in WHERE predicates give the best file pruning. Low cardinality columns give little pruning, equality joins don't benefit, and IDENTITY columns can't be used.
